blocks.content: By now you have gone through the three way handshake, the four way close, sequence numbers, acknowledgments, sliding window, and retransmission, six topics that together explain how TCP turns an unreliable network into a reliable one. This chapter does something different from the rest of the module. It does not teach anything new.

Instead, this is a fast, rapid fire review of the exact questions about TCP that come up again and again in real technical interviews. Every question here points back to a full topic elsewhere in this module, and every answer is written to be clean, confident, and complete enough to stand on its own. Treat this chapter as a self check. If any answer here feels even slightly shaky, that shakiness is the signal, go back and reread the full topic it points to before moving on.

Before the rapid fire questions start, here is the whole module compressed into a single table. Six topics, six one line takeaways. If you can look at this table and immediately explain the reasoning behind every row without hesitating, you are in genuinely strong shape for a TCP interview.

blocks.title: How to actually use this chapter
blocks.content: Do not just read the answers below and nod along. Try answering each question yourself first, out loud or on paper, before reading the given answer. The gap between what you can explain unprompted and what you recognize when you read it is exactly the gap an interviewer will find.
2. Why Does TCP Need Three Steps to Open a Connection?
blocks.text: 2. Why Does TCP Need Three Steps to Open a Connection?

blocks.content: This is probably the single most asked TCP question in interviews, and the trap is answering it with just a description of the three steps instead of the reasoning behind them. The real answer is about confirmation in both directions, not just three arbitrary messages.

A connection is only genuinely ready when both sides know two things about the other side, that it exists, and that it can hear them. Two steps are not enough for that. If the client sends a SYN and the server replies with a SYN ACK, the client now knows the server is alive and listening. But the server does not yet know its own reply actually reached the client, so from the server side, the connection is still not confirmed. The third step, the client sending its ACK, is what closes that final gap and gives the server its own proof.

So each side ends up sending exactly one SYN, confirming it is ready to talk, and each side ends up sending exactly one acknowledgment, confirming it heard the other side. That is four pieces of information in total, but the server folds its own SYN and ACK into a single SYN ACK segment, which is why it only takes three actual messages, not four, to carry that same information across the wire.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215558-517568466.png
blocks.alt: Why Does TCP Need Three Steps to Open a Connection?

blocks.content: 3. Why Does Closing a Connection Take Four Steps, and What Is TIME_WAIT?
blocks.text: 3. Why Does Closing a Connection Take Four Steps, and What Is TIME_WAIT?

blocks.content: Closing feels like it should be the reverse of opening, so a natural guess is three steps again. But a TCP connection is actually two independent one way streams bundled together, one from client to server and one from server to client, and each direction has to be closed on its own.

When one side sends a FIN, it is only saying I am done sending, not I am done listening. The other side acknowledges that FIN immediately, but it might still have its own data left to send, so it keeps the connection open in that direction until it is genuinely finished too, at which point it sends its own separate FIN. That is four steps in total, FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK, two full close operations, each with its own request and its own confirmation.

TIME_WAIT is the state the side that closed first sits in after sending its final ACK. It cannot simply vanish right away, because that final ACK might get lost, and the other side, still waiting for it, might resend its own FIN. TIME_WAIT keeps the connection details around for a fixed period specifically so a resent FIN can still be answered correctly, instead of arriving at a connection that no longer exists.

blocks.title: Why TIME_WAIT actually matters in production
blocks.content: TIME_WAIT sounds like a minor detail until you are running a server handling thousands of connections a second. Each one leaves a TIME_WAIT entry behind for a couple of minutes, and at high enough volume those entries can pile up faster than they expire, quietly exhausting available ports or memory. It is a textbook example of a small protocol detail becoming a real operational concern at scale.

blocks.alt: Why Does Closing a Connection Take Four Steps, and What Is TIME_WAIT?

blocks.content: 4. What Do Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgment Numbers Actually Count?
blocks.text: 4. What Do Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgment Numbers Actually Count?

blocks.content: This is the question that separates people who memorized the three way handshake diagram from people who actually understand TCP. The sequence number does not count segments, packets, or messages. It counts bytes. Every single byte in the data stream has its own position, and the sequence number on a segment is simply the position of the first byte inside that segment.

That is why sequence numbers jump by different amounts between segments. A segment carrying 1000 bytes starting at sequence number 5000 will be followed by a segment starting at sequence number 6000, not 5001. The gap between consecutive sequence numbers is literally the byte length of the segment before it, a detail that trips up a lot of people who assume it just increments by one each time.

The acknowledgment number works off that same byte level counting, but it means something slightly different, and precisely. It names the next byte the receiver expects, which automatically confirms every byte before it as successfully received. If a receiver sends back ack=6000, that is not just confirming one segment, it is a blanket statement that every byte up to and including byte 5999 has arrived safely. This cumulative property is exactly what makes TCP acknowledgment efficient, one number can confirm an entire run of data at once.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215558-730305090.png
blocks.alt: What Do Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgment Numbers Actually Count?

blocks.content: 5. How Does TCP Recover From a Lost Segment?
blocks.text: 5. How Does TCP Recover From a Lost Segment?

blocks.content: TCP has exactly two distinct ways of noticing and fixing loss, and interviewers specifically want to hear both named and told apart, not blended together into one vague answer about resending data.

The first is timeout retransmission, the fallback that always works. Every segment sent starts a retransmission timer, and if no acknowledgment for it arrives before that timer expires, TCP assumes it was lost and resends it. This is reliable but slow, because it depends on waiting out the full timer duration with no other signal to act on.

The second is fast retransmission, and it is the clever optimization. When a segment arrives out of order because an earlier one went missing, the receiver keeps resending the same acknowledgment number, the one still waiting on that missing piece, instead of staying silent. Once the sender sees three duplicate acknowledgments for the same number in a row, it treats that as a strong enough signal of loss on its own, and resends the missing segment immediately, without waiting for the timer to expire at all. It is a targeted, fast reaction built entirely out of a pattern in the acknowledgments the sender was already receiving.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215559-639346507.png
blocks.alt: How Does TCP Recover From a Lost Segment?

blocks.content: 6. Why a Sliding Window Instead of Stop and Wait?
blocks.text: 6. Why a Sliding Window Instead of Stop and Wait?

blocks.content: Imagine sending one letter at a time and refusing to write the next one until you get a reply confirming the last one arrived. That is stop and wait, and it technically works, but it wastes almost all of your time sitting idle, waiting on a reply that has to cross the network and come back before you are allowed to do anything else.

The sliding window fixes exactly that waste. Instead of one segment in flight at a time, the sender is allowed to have many segments outstanding simultaneously, up to whatever window size the receiver has advertised, all of them unacknowledged at once. As acknowledgments come back for the oldest data, the window slides forward, opening up room to send new data further ahead. Throughput stops being limited by round trip time on every single segment, and becomes limited instead by how much data can be in flight at once.

This single change is the difference between TCP being usable on a real network with real latency and TCP being unbearably slow. On a connection with even a modest round trip time, sending one segment and waiting for its acknowledgment before sending the next could mean spending the vast majority of total transfer time simply waiting, which is precisely the inefficiency the sliding window exists to eliminate.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215559-79677350.png
blocks.alt: Why a Sliding Window Instead of Stop and Wait?

blocks.content: 7. Flow Control vs Congestion Control, Restated
blocks.text: 7. Flow Control vs Congestion Control, Restated

blocks.content: This pairing gets confused constantly, enough that it deserves a direct, quick restatement here even though both get their own full topics in the Transport Layer part of this module. The short version is who is being protected.

Flow control protects the receiver. It exists so a fast sender cannot overwhelm a slower receiver buffer, and the receiver enforces it directly by advertising how much space it currently has available. Congestion control protects the network itself. It exists so senders collectively do not overwhelm the shared links and routers in between, and unlike flow control, no single receiver enforces it, the sender has to infer network conditions from signals like loss and adjust its own sending rate accordingly.

8. Three Questions That Separate Understanding From Memorization
blocks.text: 8. Three Questions That Separate Understanding From Memorization

blocks.content: The questions so far test whether you know what each mechanism is. These next three test whether you actually understand how the mechanisms behave in situations slightly outside the textbook description, which is exactly what a good interviewer probes for once the basics are confirmed.

What happens if that very last ACK in the three way handshake gets lost. Walk through it slowly. The client believes the connection is fully established the moment it sends that ACK, so it moves on and may even start sending data. But the server never received it, so the server is still sitting in the SYN_RECEIVED state, from its perspective the handshake never actually finished. Eventually the server own retransmission timer expires, and since it never got its ACK, it resends its SYN ACK, effectively asking the client to acknowledge again.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215560-256937738.png
blocks.alt: Three Questions That Separate Understanding From Memorization

blocks.content: Can a connection keep receiving data in one direction after the other direction has already sent its FIN. Yes, and this is a direct consequence of the four way close being built from two independent directions. A FIN only ever says that one side is finished sending. It says nothing about the other direction, so the side that receives a FIN can perfectly well keep transmitting its own data for a while, and the side that sent the FIN keeps acknowledging that incoming data normally, right up until the second side finally sends its own FIN and the connection fully closes.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215560-858209557.png
blocks.alt: Three Questions That Separate Understanding From Memorization

blocks.content: If a receiver acknowledgment number stays exactly the same across several packets in a row, what does that specifically tell you. It means there is a gap in the byte stream at that exact point, some earlier segment has not arrived yet, and because acknowledgment numbers are cumulative, the receiver cannot move that number forward past the missing piece no matter what arrives after it. This is not a vague symptom, it is the precise trigger condition for fast retransmission, three duplicate acknowledgments for the same number is the sender signal that a specific segment needs resending right now.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437215561-247954207.png
blocks.alt: Three Questions That Separate Understanding From Memorization

blocks.title: Why interviewers keep asking variations of this
blocks.content: Questions like these are popular precisely because a memorized definition of fast retransmission does not help you answer them. You have to actually trace what each side knows and does not know at each point in time. That tracing ability, not the vocabulary, is what the question is really testing.

blocks.title: The advice that actually helps in interviews
blocks.content: The strongest answers in TCP interviews consistently connect a mechanism to the specific problem it solves, instead of just reciting its name and definition. Anyone can say TCP uses fast retransmission. Being able to explain why duplicate acknowledgments specifically signal loss, not just that they do, is what separates a strong answer from a shallow, memorized one. Every answer in this chapter was written to model that habit, always land on the reasoning, not just the name.

Step back and look at what this module actually built, end to end. It opened with the three way handshake, establishing a connection both sides had genuinely confirmed. It moved through sequence numbers, giving every single byte in the stream an exact, trackable position. It added acknowledgments, a cumulative signal letting one number confirm an entire run of received data. It introduced the sliding window, turning that reliable exchange from a slow, one segment at a time crawl into a genuinely fast pipeline. It covered retransmission, the two ways TCP actually notices and repairs real loss on a real, imperfect network. And it closed with the four way termination, unwinding that same connection cleanly, one independent direction at a time.

That is TCP complete reliability machinery, traced from first principles all the way to the very last acknowledgment. None of these six pieces work in isolation, sequence numbers are meaningless without acknowledgments to respond to them, the sliding window only works because retransmission exists to catch what it loses, and the whole connection only means anything because the handshake and termination give it a clean, well understood beginning and end. If every question in this chapter felt solid, that is a genuine sign this module has landed.
10. Key Takeaways

["Three steps to open a connection because both sides need confirmation in both directions, not just one","Four steps to close because the two directions of a connection close completely independently","Sequence numbers count bytes, not segments or packets, and mark the first byte of each segment","Acknowledgment numbers are cumulative, confirming every byte up to and including the number just before the one named","Loss is recovered two ways, a slow guaranteed timeout, or a fast targeted retransmission from duplicate acknowledgments","The sliding window allows many segments in flight at once, which is what makes TCP fast instead of stop and wait slow","Flow control protects the receiver's buffer, congestion control protects the shared network, different problems entirely","TIME_WAIT exists so a lost final acknowledgment can still be answered correctly, and it matters more at scale than it looks","The strongest interview answers always explain why a mechanism exists, not just what it is called"]
